passages.original: qui cum quereretur quod iuvenis interiret, responsum ei ab incerto ferunt numine neminem plus esse victurum, quare etiamsi centum et viginti quinque annos Claudius vixisset, ne necessariam quidem mortem eius exspectandam fuisse, ut Tullius de Scipione loquitur, stupenda et mirabilis docet vita. quid enim magnum vir ille domi forisque non habuit? amavit parentes; quid mirum? amavit et fratres ; iam potest dignum esse miraculo, amavit propinquos ;
passages.english: When he complained that he was dying young, they say an answer was given him by some uncertain divinity, that no one would live longer; so, even if Claudius had lived a hundred and twenty-five years, his death, not even [as] a necessary one, ought not to have been waited for, as Tullius says of Scipio; this his astonishing and marvellous life shows. For what great quality did that man not have at home and abroad? He loved his parents: what wonder [in that]? He loved his brothers too: now it can be worthy of marvel. He loved his relatives:
passages.notes: 'Qui' (he who complained) refers to Moses, mentioned in the preceding context as having lived 125 years; 'quereretur' is a variant spelling of 'quaereretur'. The construction 'ne necessariam quidem mortem eius exspectandam fuisse' is compressed, following Cicero ('Tullius') on Scipio. The sense is probably that one ought not to have waited even for his natural death, i.e. he deserved never to die. The rendering is somewhat uncertain. 'dam- navit' in the following context is a line-break split of 'damnavit'.

passages.original: Hos igitur Claudius ingenita illa virtute superavit, hos brevi tempore adtrivit, de his vix aliquos ad patrium solum redire permisit, rogo, quantum pretium est clipeus in Curia tantae victoriae? quantum una aurea statua? dicit Ennius de Scipione : Quantam statuam faciet populus Romanus, quantam colum- nam, quae res tuas gestas loquatur? possumus dicere Flavium Claudium, unicum in terris principem, non columnis, non statuis sed famae viribus adiuvari.
passages.english: These, then, Claudius overcame by that inborn valour of his; these he wore down in a short time; of these he allowed scarcely any to return to their native soil. What, I ask, is a shield in the Senate-house worth as the price of so great a victory? What is a single golden statue worth? Ennius says of Scipio: "How great a statue will the Roman people make, how great a column, to tell of your deeds?" We can say that Flavius Claudius, the one prince on earth, is sustained not by columns, not by statues, but by the strength of his fame.
passages.notes: "colum- nam" is a line-break split for "columnam". The Ennius quotation is given as the text has it; the original fragment may have been verse, and its wording here may be adapted.
